draft.title: Business models
card: A business model is how a business reaches its customers and makes money. One business can use more than one model.
Online
sells through a website or app, so customers can buy without visiting a shop. Direct-to-consumer means the maker sells straight to the customer, with no retailer in between.
Bricks-and-mortar
sells from a physical site such as a shop or café, where customers come in to buy.
Franchise

the owner of a brand (the franchisor) lets others (franchisees) run outlets under that brand. Franchisees usually pay fees. An importer buys goods from overseas to sell locally. An exporter sells goods overseas.
draft.remember: A business model is the way a business reaches customers and earns money.

a.q: Which business is using a franchise model?
opts: Sam pays a brand owner to run a store under its name
Sam sells her own jam from a stall at a local market
Sam buys tea from Sri Lanka and sells it in Victoria
Sam sells her own soap to customers through her website
a.why: In a franchise, Sam runs an outlet under a brand owner's name and pays fees. Selling at a market stall is bricks-and-mortar style selling under her own name, not a franchise. Importing is about buying from overseas.
a.clue: Look for someone running an outlet under another owner's brand.

b.q: Priya's company in Geelong makes running shoes. It sells them only on its own website and posts them straight to customers. Which model best describes this?
opts: Direct-to-consumer and online
Franchise and bricks-and-mortar
Importer and bricks-and-mortar
Exporter and franchise
b.why: Priya's company makes the shoes and sells them straight to buyers, so it is direct-to-consumer. It sells through a website, so it is online. Nothing says it sells overseas or runs a shop, so exporter and bricks-and-mortar do not fit.
b.clue: Who makes the shoes, who sells them, and where does the sale happen?

a.best: Sam pays a brand owner to run a store under its name

problems.detail: Importer and exporter are defined inside the franchise bullet, and direct-to-consumer inside the online bullet. Students could think importing and exporting are part of franchising, or that direct-to-consumer only happens online. Each model would be clearer in its own bullet.
The clue ('someone running an outlet under another owner's brand') closely paraphrases the right option ('run a store under its name'), so a student can match the wording without knowing the idea.

check.summary: Both answers are correct and unambiguous. Fix two things: the card puts importer/exporter in the franchise bullet and direct-to-consumer in the online bullet, which may confuse students, and question a's clue nearly restates the right option.

proposal.title: Business models
card: A business model is how a business reaches customers and makes money. An online business sells through a website or app. A bricks-and-mortar business sells from a physical site, such as a shop or café.
Direct-to-consumer
the maker sells straight to its customers, with no retailer in between. This can happen online, in the maker's own shop, or both.
Franchise
a brand owner (the franchisor) lets others (franchisees) run outlets under its brand. Franchisees usually pay fees for this.
Importer or exporter
an importer buys goods from overseas to sell in Australia. An exporter sells goods to buyers in other countries.
proposal.remember: Many businesses combine models, such as a maker selling direct-to-consumer through its own website.
